dimension_description: Youngs modulus describes linear elastic stiffness, the ratio of stress to strain for small reversible deformations. It is the slope of the initial part of a stress strain curve under uniaxial load at stated temperature and rate. Microstructure, porosity, and moisture can shift it dramatically for natural materials. Each value below includes a representative condition so comparisons hold water.

items.description: Polymer foams behave like springs in a scaffold of cells, so their effective modulus is tiny until densification. Cell size, gas content, and skin layers matter as much as chemistry. Designers tune this for pillows versus helmet liners. The value is for a flexible open cell foam in small strain compression.

items.description: Cartilage combines a collagen network with pressurized water to form a poroelastic material with low instantaneous modulus. Under sustained load the modulus rises as fluid drains. Healthy joints depend on this time dependence for shock absorption. The value is an initial small strain tangent.

items.description: Soft rubber stores little energy per strain because chains uncoil easily, leading to a very low modulus. As strain rises, entropic elasticity stiffens the response. Fillers like carbon black raise the modulus by reinforcing the network. The value given is for an unfilled gum rubber at room temperature.

items.description: Silica aerogel is often called solid smoke because its density is so low and its stiffness is only modestly above that of soft foams. Even so, it is a true solid with a measurable elastic slope that matters in insulation panels and particle collectors. Large strains quickly move it beyond the small-strain regime. The value is a representative low-density aerogel modulus.

items.description: Cork compresses easily at first because gas-filled cells collapse and recover, which is why it works so well as a bottle stopper and vibration isolator. Its modulus is far above a liquid but far below wood or plastic. Moisture and direction both matter because the cell structure is anisotropic. The value is a representative small-strain modulus.

items.description: Polyethylene is flexible because its elastic modulus is only a few hundred megapascals, several hundred times lower than common metals. That makes it ideal for bottles, cutting boards, and films that need to bend without cracking. Crystallinity shifts the stiffness a bit but not the basic scale. The value is representative for HDPE.

items.description: Tendon stores elastic energy for locomotion with a modulus around a gigapascal that rises with strain. Warm tissues display higher extensibility and lower stiffness initially. Training induces remodeling that tunes this property. The figure is a small strain slope for Achilles tendon.

items.description: Softwoods are anisotropic; along the grain the modulus is moderate, across the grain it is an order lower. Moisture acts like a plasticizer that reduces stiffness. Builders season wood to stabilize this property. The value is longitudinal for dried spruce.

items.description: ABS plastic is noticeably stiffer than polyethylene but still far softer than metals, which is why product housings feel solid while retaining some impact tolerance. Engineers like this middle ground for consumer goods and machine covers. The modulus depends on temperature and whether the part is molded or printed. The value is a common handbook figure.

items.description: Nylon sits in the low-gigapascal range, stiff enough for gears, fasteners, and bushings yet compliant enough to damp shock and noise. Moisture softens it because water acts as a plasticizer in the polymer network. That is why dry and conditioned values can differ noticeably in datasheets. The value is a representative small-strain modulus for nylon 6.

items.description: PLA prints feel rigid because their elastic modulus reaches a few gigapascals, substantially above many household plastics. That helps small printed parts keep shape, though it does not guarantee toughness. Temperature softening remains the main weakness. The number is a representative modulus for solid PLA.

items.description: Water ice is much less stiff than rock or metal but far stiffer than rubber, which is why glaciers can support cracks and transmit seismic waves even while creeping over years. Planetary scientists rely on this modulus when modeling icy moons and ice shelves. Temperature shifts it meaningfully. The value is a typical terrestrial ice modulus.

items.description: Spider dragline silk stretches more than most engineering fibers, but its modulus still lands around tens of gigapascals, high enough to store useful elastic energy in a light thread. Biologists care because that balance of stiffness and toughness is rare in natural materials. Humidity changes the feel quickly. The value is a representative dry-fiber modulus.

items.description: Hardwoods like oak are stiffer than many softwoods because of their denser microstructure and higher latewood fraction. Furniture makers and structural engineers both feel this directly in how little a board flexes under load. Grain direction still dominates the number, so this is an along-grain figure. The value is a representative modulus for oak.

items.description: Common fired brick behaves like a stiff brittle ceramic composite on small elastic strains. Masonry design often treats whole walls rather than brick alone, but the brick material itself lives in the low tens of gigapascals. That is enough to keep arches and facades from sagging visibly under ordinary loads. The value is a representative engineering brick modulus.

items.description: Lead is soft in yield strength but not infinitely floppy: its elastic modulus still sits in the tens of gigapascals. That is why lead pipes and sheets can hold shape until creep and plasticity take over. The contrast between low modulus metals and high modulus ceramics is one of the simplest material lessons to feel by hand. The value is a standard handbook number.

Its geometry makes it especially effective for lightweight columns and scaffolds. Across the grain the modulus is far lower, so direction matters. The number is an along-fiber representative value.

Implant designers choose alloys to match this to avoid stress shielding. The value is for human femoral cortical bone in tension.

items.description: Magnesium alloys are attractive in vehicles and aircraft because their stiffness is lower than aluminum’s but their density is lower too. That means components can still achieve respectable specific stiffness when geometry is optimized. Corrosion protection and fatigue remain important design constraints. The value is a representative modulus for structural magnesium alloys.

items.description: Kevlar fibers are less stiff than carbon fibers but still very much engineering fibers, landing around tens of gigapascals in axial modulus. Their real advantage is the combination of stiffness, toughness, and low density. Ballistic fabrics and ropes turn that combination into practical products. The value is a representative fiber-direction modulus.

items.description: Copper combines excellent electrical conduction with a modulus a bit above one hundred gigapascals, enough to make busbars and springs hold form while still yielding more readily than steels. Purity and cold work change strength much more than stiffness. That separation is why electrical and mechanical design tables both matter. The value is a representative modulus for bulk copper.

The exact value depends on crystal direction because the lattice is anisotropic. Semiconductor fabrication treats this as a design parameter, not trivia. The number is a representative orientation-averaged modulus.

items.description: Tungsten is one of the stiffest practical metals, which is why it holds shape at heat and finds use in filaments, weights, and tooling. Its density is famous, but the high modulus is just as important in applications that need resistance to elastic bending. Brittleness is the tradeoff. The value is a representative room-temperature modulus.

items.description: Silicon carbide combines ceramic hardness with very high elastic stiffness, making it valuable for armor, abrasives, mirrors, and high-temperature components. Components made from it resist small elastic strain strongly before brittle failure becomes the real limit. It is a good reminder that stiffness and toughness are separate traits. The value is a representative engineering modulus.

units.description: Pascals are the base unit for elastic modulus, connecting stress and strain directly. Reporting in pascals keeps comparisons across metals, polymers, and tissues coherent. Engineers often translate to gigapascals for brevity. All item values are stored in pascals before conversion.
units.name: pascals

units.description: Gigapascals compress the large numbers typical of stiffness into two or three digits. Most structural materials live between one and three hundred gigapascals. Using GPa matches handbooks and FEA software defaults. Convert by multiplying pascals by 1e-9.
units.name: gigapascals

units.description: Megapascals are useful when discussing softer materials like polymers, tissues, and foams. They align with biomedical and consumer product literature. Conversions from pascals are linear and exact. The unit bridges daily lab work with engineering design.
units.name: megapascals
